international.title: Milburn calls for welfare state ‘revolution’ as landmark youth unemployment report to be published – UK politics live
international.summary: Alan Milburn says his plan could cut the welfare bill before the next election, but overall savings will take years Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people This is what the opposition parties have been saying about the Alan Milburn proposals. The full report has not formally been published yet, but it has been circulating in Westminster on an embargoed basis since yesterday and so the parties all know what it says. The Conservatives says Milburn should be cutting welfare more aggressively. This is from Helen Whately , the shadow work and pensions secretary. Conservatives agree with Alan Milburn on the problem, and we want his review to succeed. Where Milburn gets it right, we’ll back him. Especially where he adopts our proposals like shifting from cash sickness benefits to support for milder conditions and cutting national insurance for young people. Alan Milburn is right to criticise the tax and regulation burdens Labour have imposed on businesses. But his review is too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state. Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now - because nothing will happen for at least three years. Successive governments have allowed a generation to fall through the cracks. Nearly a million young people are now out of work or training, which is more than there are job vacancies in the entire country. ‘Work not welfare’ means nothing when the work simply isn’t there. If ministers want to halve the number of Neets by 2036, they need a plan for growth. That means scrapping Labour’s jobs tax, joining the EU single market and cutting the cost of doing business, so firms can afford to hire young people again. No target or guarantee can conjure up jobs that don’t exist. Alan Milburn’s call to cut the cost of hiring for employers is a glaring admission Labour’s jobs tax has failed. It destroyed opportunities for workers, and particularly youngsters. Huge amounts of damage could have been avoided if Labour listened to the warnings. Waiting 10 years to fix the youth jobs crisis is a huge missed opportunity. We would be consigning another generation to the scrap heap. What we’ve seen so far from the Blair-era minister and adviser to private equity firms is extremely concerning. There is an alternative to threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, an alternative to unsuitable short-term work. Andy Burnham promised an end to 40 years of neoliberalism, but this is more of the same tired proposals. The Green party’s true alternative is proper work and training for proper pay, so young people can reach their full potential without the threat of poverty and homelessness. Continue reading...
